sc.prose: Likely the earliest traditionally-dateable sound change in Carite, and in Indo-European in general, is ::laryngeal colouring::. As its traces can be seen even within Anatolian, it is likely that an allophonic process of vowel colouring next to the laryngeals _*h₂ *h₃_ predates the split of the Anatolian subfamily. Early on, this had little effect on the morphology of Indo-European; only later did it influence its grammatical ablaut. Compare the following examples:

Obstruent clusters undergo ::regressive voicing assimilation::. This process is also extremely early, though its age relative to laryngeal voicing cannot be determined. Observe the following examples:

This change also operated when the cluster included aspirates: they can be assumed to also be voiced, or breathily/partially voiced, to begin with. All aspirates in such clusters presumably become voiceless aspirates, but their result cannot be shown to be different from regular voiced obstruents: presumably, this aspiration is lost early enough internally to merge their outcome with that of regular _tenues_, and not (the somewhat later) voiceless aspirates.

Later on, s-mobile arose and proliferated. This had a different behavior, promoting progressive voicing assimilation under ::Siebs' Law::. This had the effect of changing morphological |*sB *sBh| into |*sP|:
sc.prose_after: It is not clear if the voiceless aspirates remained phonemic for long — in any case, in Carite, they behave identically to the regular voiceless tenues and presumably merged shortly after if they ever were distinct in the first place.

sc.prose: As part of the ::degemination of dentals::, the first dental (i.e. alveolar plosive) was affricated, likely already in Proto-Indo-European times, and then the resulting cluster was simplified:
sc.prose_after:
This process continued to be a productive morphophonological alternation.
This development mirrors the degemination in Greek:
- pie@bʰéydʰtis@bʰéy::dʰt::is > °BHIDHTIS°, grc@πίστις@πί::στ::ις=pí::st::is;
Compare this to Italic, Celtic and Germanic, where the degemination of dentals resulted in _*ss_:
- pie@sedtós@se::dt::ós > pgmc@sessaz@se::ss::az, lat@sessus@se::ss::us;
- pie@medtós@me::dt::ós > pclt@messos@me::ss::os.
It is likely the change was not complete yet in Celtic in Proto-Celtic times, as we find an intermediate stage in Gaulish.

sc.prose: The treatment of ::thorn clusters:: sets Common Indo-European apart from Early Indo-European: none of these languages preserve them intact, i.e. as coronal-dorsal clusters. In Carite, thorn clusters underwent metathesis:
sc.prose_after:
Metathesis of thorn clusters is a trait shared with Celtic and Greek as shown below:
- pie@dʰǵʰési@::dʰǵʰ::ési > °YESTERDAYWORD° (through _*gdesi_), pclt@gdesi@::gd::esi, grc@χθές@::χθ::ές=::khth::és.
The assibilation of the dental in °YESTERDAYWORD° will be discussed later. In the other western branches, the clusters were simply reduced:
- pie@dʰǵʰemelos@::dʰǵʰ::emelos > lat@humilis@::h::umilis; compare to °LOWWW° and grc@χθαμαλός@::χθ::αμαλός=::khth::amalós;
- pie@dʰǵʰésros@::dʰǵʰ::ésros > pgmc@gestraz@::g::estraz.

sc.prose: Another early process in Carite history, shared with Italo-Celtic, Greek, and probably Germanic, is ::Osthoff's Law::: long vowels shorten when preceding a resonant that's followed by a consonant:
sc.prose_after:
Osthoff's Law continued to be productive until after the loss of laryngeals in all branches, but in Carite, it acted as a surface filter for a particularly long time, continuing to affect later loans and formations all the way until the loss of vowel length in the medieval period. The example below illustrates how it divides western Indo-European from eastern languages such as Sanskrit:
- pie@tpḗrsneh₂@tp::ḗ::rsneh₂ > °HEEL1°, grc@πτέρνη@πτ::έ::ρνη=pt::é::rnē, lat@perna@p::e::rna, pgmc@fersnō@f::e::rsnō; compare to san@पार्ष्णि=pā́rṣṇi.
In subsequent changes, Osthoff's Law, as a surface filter, will continue to be pointed out.

sc.prose: Laryngeals between a resonant and a consonant were lost, provided that the resonant was preceded by _*o_; this is known as the ::Saussure Effect::. While it is unclear if this effect already affected Proto-Indo-European proper or if it's a later development, it is nonetheless shared by many branches, Carite included:
Centumisation in Carite took place somewhat late, and only after the ::coalescence:: of a sequence of a back velar followed by _*w_ into a single labiovelar consonant:
sc.prose_after: It is worth noting that Greek, in order to preserve the length caused by the original cluster, rendered them as geminates instead.

sc.prose: The typical actual centumisation involved the unconditional merger of the palatovelars into regular velars as follows:

The Proto-Indo-European laryngeals, which (mostly) disappeared in almost all branches, left behind traces before doing so. Besides the laryngeal colouring mentioned earlier, which was presumably much older, the ::first laryngeal loss:: marks the start of a long process of laryngeal deletion:
sc.prose_after: As Osthoff's Law continued to be in effect, vowels were prevented from being lengthened if they were followed by a resonant and another consonant.

sc.prose: Syllabic sonorants and laryngeals adjacent to them interacted in many branches, Carite included. Similar to Celtic, Greek and Latin, Carite inserted a prop vowel between any syllabic sonorant and a laryngeal, moving the syllabicity from the sonorant to this new prop vowel:

Next, syllabic sonorants lost their syllabicity with an epenthetic vowel _*ǝ_ being inserted to compensate. The exact resolution depended on the environment. Syllabic nasals turned into _*a_ when preceded by at least two consonants, while syllabic liquids inserted a prop vowel after them in the same environment. All remaining syllabic sonorants simply ejected a prop vowel before them:
sc.prose_after: It is likely that the reflex of nasals before clusters started off as a nasalised neutral vowel - _*ə̃_ - which later lost its nasalisation and neutralised differently than its oral equivalent, most importantly not engaging in the vowel colouring that would later take place.

sc.prose: Whenever a laryngeal was surrounded by two true consonants - that is, all consonants excluding the semivowels _*y *w_ - it inserted a prop vowel after itself:
The precise reflex of the recently created prop vowels heavily depended on their environment. First of all, it took up rounding from any previous consonant:
Due to the regressive action of the _boukolos_ rule, which delabialised labiovelars next to _*u_, this delabialised any labiovelar after which it occured:
sc.prose_after: It is worth noting that this did not affect new sequences of _*wu_, which stayed as is.

sc.prose: The prop vowel took colour from surrounding laryngeals much like older _*e_:
Finally, any remaining prop vowels merged into _*u_ when directly preceding _*m_, while all other prop vowels lost their distinctiveness by merging into _*i_:
An unusual but well-documented Carite change is the effect of laryngeals on consonants in word-initial position. They voiced plosives and sibilants, probably through a process of glottalisation:

Similarly, semivowels underwent fortition, with _*y_ surfacing as _*k_ and _*w_ surfacing as _*kʷ_. Importantly, however, is that the fortition of _*y_ only took place following _*h₁_, as opposed to the other consonants, which underwent this change regardless of which of laryngeal:
sc.prose_after:
A longstanding hypothesis is that the fortition of _*h₁y_ resulted in _*ḱ_, which hadn't merged into _*k_ yet. This opinion is somewhat controversial, but is unfalsifiable because what sound exactly that _*y_ fortited to is impossible to know for sure. The fact only _*h₁_ affected _*y_ is in line with its word-initial treatment in Greek and can be explained through Byrd's improvement of Pinault's Law; this would imply _*h₂ *h₃_ would have been lost before _*y_ before this phonological change could have taken place. For more information, please refer to §Bozzone1§.
This change is occasionally termed ::Engels' Law::, and it was first posited by the Limburgish philologist Klaus Engels.

sc.prose: It is likely that at this point, the laryngeals lost differentiation and merged into one general laryngeal continuant, completing the ::merger of laryngeals:::
The next loss of laryngeals (::second laryngeal loss::) happened to sequences of vowels with a laryngeal:
sc.prose_after: The lengthening of contracted laryngeal sequences still obeyed Osthoff's Law, shortening the new vowels when followed by a sequence of a resonant plus obstruent. Examples of this process are scant, but they are evident in the so-called conjunctive nominals, which, in early Carite, take special forms in subordinate clauses and in coordinated clauses. A typical example of this is with the masculine noun °EKWOS°: its genitive plural is attested as both the ordinary εκῠωμ (_ekwōm_) and the conjunctive εκῠομφε (_ekwomfe_) - the length of the vowel in the suffix is indicative of Osthoff's Law. With the deletion of the laryngeal and subsequent compensatory lengthening, any allophonous colouring effects were phonemicised.

sc.prose: After this, the laryngeals failed to effect any further changes, and were likely lost shortly thereafter, completing the ::third laryngeal loss:::
sc.prose_after: This included all word-initial laryngeals immediately followed by a consonant, which were lost in all daughters except for Anatolian, Greek, Armenian, and Phrygian. It is worth noting this change phonemicised what used to be allophones; i.e. the colouring of _*e_ and Engels' Law.

sc.prose: One of the longstanding issues in the evolution from Proto-Indo-European to Abean was the surfacing of some _*e *ē_ as _*a *ā_. This shift is called ::Davide's Law::, and it must have taken place following the dissolution of syllabic sonorants and laryngeals, but before the collapse of the three-way plosive system and (presumably) the fricativisation of the labiovelars. Davide's Law posits that pretonic _*e *ē_ shift to _*a *ā_ when next to a rhotic, the semivowel _*w_ or its vocalic equivalent _*u_, and any (labio)velar:
When preceding _*n_ before another velar, the allophonic velarity of the nasal also triggered the same shift:
sc.prose_after:
It is likely this change originally also affected the augment for roots starting with the consonants mentioned above, but we find no trace of this in inscriptions, and it was probably analogised away later.
Due to the environment this change is conditioned by, several historical linguists have pointed out the noteworthy similarity to the phenomenon known as RUKI, which was long held to only affect satem languages. However, post-Proto-Germanic developments related to vowel lowering in RUKI-like environments have pointed towards the isogloss being shared with at least one centum language, too (see §Prescott0§), so it is not unthinkable that the Carite shift may be explained in the same vein.

sc.prose: Unusually, some words show the effects of Davide's Law outside of these conditions. One of these conditions is after initial _*s_, which will actually be explained shortly; the others are more opaque. The effect again seems to be limited to pretonic _*e *ē_, but the range of adjacent consonants triggering it seems to be larger. Some Caritologists have suggested that dialectally, Davide's Law also affected any pretonic _*e *ē_ next to voiced obstruents, citing the glottalic theory as a possible additional cause. Regardless, the conditions are not fully understood and we only posit the following:
sc.prose_after: Superficially, the fact Carite exhibits “too many” a-vocalisms is noteworthily similar to an identical problem in Latin. However, the conditions are entirely different. For more information on the Italic colouring of _*o_ to _*a_, please refer to sources such as §Vine3§ and §de Vaan1§.

sc.prose: Word-initial laryngeal voicing of _*s_ enables the dating of another change: its word-initial, prevocalic debuccalisation:
sc.prose_after:
Greek also took part in the debuccalisation of _*s_, although it was significantly more widespread, also taking place intervocalically and in some complex clusters. Compare the following:
- pie@supnós@::s::upnós > °HUPNOS°, pclt@sownos@::s::ownos, grc@ὕπνος@::ὕ::πνος=::h::úpnos, lat@somnus@::s::omnus, pgmc@swefnaz@::s::wefnaz;
- pie@sweḱrúh₂@::s::weḱrúh₂ > °SOCRUSAUNT°, pclt@swekrū@::s::wekrū, grc@ἑκυρά@::ἑ::κυρά=::h::ekurá, lat@socrus@::s::ocrus, pgmc@swegrū@::s::wegrū.
As shown above, original _*sw-_ kept the sibilant as is; the labial would later possibly coalesce with the following vowel.

sc.prose: Another change, presumably happening concurrently, was the debuccalisation of word-initial prevocalic _*gʰ_:

In a handful of words, we find the effects of Davide's Law on words that etymologically started with _*s_. It is likely that the word-initial prevocalic merger of _*s_ and _*gʰ_, where the latter triggered the change, resulted in these hypercorrections.
Around this time, dental plosives following a (labio)velar plosive assibilated when not followed by another consonant.
sc.prose_after: This process was unique to Carite and can not be found in other early western Indo-European languages.

sc.prose: The three-way stop system collapsed after dental assibilation occurred. First, we find that plain and aspirated voiced stops neutralize after a nasal:
sc.prose_after: It was long assumed that an identical change occurred in Italic; however, recent evidence suggests that this must be a post-Italic development, as Umbrian lacks it. As such, even though Latin has an identical development, we must consider these to be independent (cf. §Stuart-Smith0§).

sc.prose: The three-way contrast system in plosives only took place after the aforementioned post-nasal neutralisation. The voiced aspirates, being actually breathy voiced, merged into the tenues. A glottalic interpretation is that in these early Carite stages voicing was a creaky or glottalised feature (explaining laryngeal voicing of word-initial obstruents), and that breathy segments had more in common acoustically with voiceless tenues. Alternatively, we posit that they simply devoiced first and only later lost their aspiration. Regardless, the internal history of this change is opaque, and we only posit:

Long-distance assimilation of labial _*p_ into a following _*kʷ_ happened around this period. It is unknown whether this change predated or postdated the collapse of the aspiration-based system, since there are no suitable etymologies with original _*bʰ_ and _*gʷʰ_. Examples are few but include the following:
sc.prose_after:
Italo-Celtic individually underwent a similar assimilation, the difference being that Carite requires the second labiovelar to be prevocalic, whereas Italo-Celtic does not. Compare the following:
- pie@pénkʷe@::p::én::kʷ::e > °5°, pclt@kʷenkʷe@::kʷ::en::kʷ::e, grc@πέντε@::π::έν::τ::ε=::p::én::t::e, lat@quīnque@::qu::īn::qu::e, pgmc@fimfe@::f::im::f::e;
- pie@pokʷtéh₂@::p::o::kʷ::téh₂ > °COCTUSSWEAT°; compare to pclt@kʷoxtos@::kʷ::o::x::tos (through _*::kʷ::o::k::tos_), lat@coctus@::c::o::c::tus (through _::qu::o::c::tus_).
The development of pgmc@fimfe seems like it fits the picture, but is actually an irregular assimilation going the other way around, with _*kʷ_ assimilating into the preceding _*p_ and a shift to _*f_ through Grimm's Law. On the preconsonantal delabialisation in the latter example, as well as the Carite outcome of _*kʷs_, see below. The Carite ordinal °5o° appears to defy the prevocalic requirement of the shift, but this is easily explained as analogy with the cardinal.

sc.prose: It was roughly at this time that the more lenis labiovelar plosives _*kʷ *gʷ_ lost their velar plosion, but retained the lower frequency timbre of velarisation by labiodentalising instead of merely shifting to labials:
sc.prose_after:
The development of labiovelars into labials (rather than labiodentals) is seen in some of Carite's sister branches. Celtic, for example, merges _*gʷ_ into _*b_ with _*gʷʰ_ taking its place. In Greek, labiovelars merged into labial or dental stops depending on their environment; the exact outcome also depends on the dialect. Latin retained _*kʷ_ as <<qu>> (except in cases where it was later unrounded), while _*gʷ_ merged into _*w_ <<v>> when not postnasal. Some other Italic languages shifted them to labial plosives. Germanic retained labialisation, but the series had been subject to Grimm's Law, yielding _*hw *kw *gw_. Compare the following cognates:
- pie@linékʷti@liné::kʷ::ti > °LEYKWOO° (through _*lin::f::ṓ_) > pclt@linkʷeti@lin::kʷ::eti, grc@λιμπάνω@λιμ::π::άνω=lim::p::ánō, lat@linquō@lin::qu::ō; pie@h₂ékʷeh₂@h₂é::kʷ::eh₂ > °AQUAWATER°, lat@aquā@a::qu::ā, pgmc@ahwō@a::hw::ō;
- pie@gʷih₃wós@::gʷ::ih₃wós > °VIVUS°, pclt@biwos@::b::iwos, lat@vīvus@::v::īvus, pgmc@kwikwaz@::kw::ikwaz; pie@h₁régʷos@h₁ré::gʷ::os > °TWILIGHTDUSK°, grc@ἔρεβος@ἔρε::β::ος=ére::b::os, pgmc@rekwaz@re::kw::az.
The intervocalic labiovelar in pgmc@kwikwaz is a development unique to Germanic referred to as Cowgill's Law; for more information, please refer to §Ringe0§.
It is worth noting that Carite, unlike all other western centum languages - Celtic (before _*y_, _*t_, _*s_ and _*n_), Greek (before _*y_), Latin (before all consonants) and Germanic (before _*y_, _*r_ _*t_) - preserved labialisation in all cases (with the obvious exception of the boukolos rule). Compare the words for “night”:
- pie@nókʷts@nó::kʷ::ts > °NUFT° (through _*no::f::sī_), pclt@noxtV-@no::x::tV-, grc@νύξ@νύ::ξ::=nú::x:: (through _nó::kʷ::ts_ > _nú::k::ts_ with Cowgill's Law), lat@nox@no::x:: (through _no::c::ts_), pgmc@nahts@na::h::ts.
Please do note that the conditions of delabialisation in the other branches mentioned above are simplifications. For further information, consult the relevant sources.

sc.prose: When any vowel was followed by _*i *u_, the sequence collapsed into a diphthong, with _*i *u_ surfacing as the semivowels _*y *w_. If they were formerly stressed, the stress shifted to the preceding vowel:
sc.prose_after: This widespread change primarily resolved hiatus originating from _*VHV_ environments.

sc.prose: Very early on, the homorganic sequence _*eye_ coalesced into a long vowel:

At some point between the coalescence of _*eye_ and all further monophthongisation (as will be discussed below), semivowel dissimilation took place. In brief, _*w_ and _*y_ shifted to _*b_ and _*l_, respectively, when near or next to another instance of the same vowel or its vocalic equivalent. More precisely, _*w_ shifted to _*b_ before _*u *ū_ or before a sequence consisting of a vowel, optionally a resonant, and _*w_, while _*y_ shifted to _*l_ before _*i *ī_ or before a sequence consisting of a vowel, optionally a resonant, and _*y_:
sc.prose_after: We know this change follows the coalescence of _*eye_, as the sequence _*-eyey_ surfaces as *-ηῐ (_*-ēj_) and not **-ελη (_*-elē_). This dissimilation did not take place where the vocalic equivalent preceded its semivowel equivalent: we find °TREEKNOWER° rather than **δρυβῑστρις (_**drubīstris_).

sc.prose: Change *y to *j to avoid confusion with the new vowel
Short diphthongs merged into long vowels. The sequences _*we *wa *wo_ collapsed too, unless the result would be shortened by Osthoff's Law.
sc.prose_after: This caused the original Indo-European ablaut patterns to become very opaque, leading to the loss of productive ablaut.

sc.prose: A few other consonant changes date to roughly this period without an easy way to precisely date them relative to other Abean developments of this time. Several clusters simplified word-initially:
In a single occurrence, word-initial _*sf-_ (from original _*skʷ-_) underwent fortition to _*sp-_:
sc.prose_after: As this appears to be the only case where said environment takes place, it is unknown whether this change is regular.

sc.prose: Likewise, initial _*dl_ dissimilates to _*gl_. This is the only attested word:
sc.prose_after: It is unknown if the same would happen to initial _*tl-_ as Abean does not appear to continue any words with it.

sc.prose: The initial cluster _*pst_ yielded Carite _*sp_, possibly through an intermediate _*spt_:
Word-initially, _*m_ was fortited to _*b_ before any liquid:
Curiously, prevocalic _*fs_ and _*ms_ both surface as _*sm_:
sc.prose_after: It is likely the cluster _*fs_ first dissimilated and merged into _*ms_ before metathesis.

sc.prose: Between two sonorants, _*s_ was deleted:
Word-finally, _*d_ rhotacised into _*r_, provided it was preceded by a vowel:
Somewhere around this time, the short high vowels _*i *u_ turned into glides when unstressed and preceding another vowel. This did not take place when following any cluster.
Following the reduction of these unstressed high vowels, dentals palatalised:
sc.prose_after: This assibilation of dentals resembles Greek, but it is by no means as widespread as in there. Refer to §Sihler0§ for the major palatalisation of most Proto-Greek consonants.

sc.prose: Stressed _*ē *ō_ were raised:
A surface filter of nasal assimilation applying across Carite history is also dated to have started here:
sc.prose_after: Exceptionally, _*m_ did not assimilate into _*n_ before _*n_, which was retained as the sequence _*mn_ instead.

sc.prose: The change that is taken to define Carite as a fully independent language in its own right is the ::Carite Verner's Law::, a structural parallel of Verner's Law in Germanic. Onsets of stressed, non-initial Carite syllables were voiced, and when distinctive positional accent was lost to fixed word-initial accent, the voicing phonemicised completely:
sc.prose_after:
The voicing is likely to have initially affected only the onset of that stressed syllable, but voicing assimilation rules for clusters spread voicing to the whole cluster. Despite the name and similar effect - that is, the voicing of segments based on now-lost accent - this law significantly differed from its Germanic analogue. In Germanic, clusters were automatically disqualified from being affected by the law, and the requirement was that the preceding syllable nucleus be unstressed. In Carite, clusters benefited significantly from the effects of this law, and it only affected the onset of what was formerly a stressed syllable as long as it was non-initial; as such, word-final coda voicing effects as in Germanic's _*-az_ suffix (from _*-os_) are nowhere to be found in Carite.
While Carite and Germanic are the most well-known examples of Indo-European branches losing phonemic stress or pitch accent only after it had functioned as conditioning for other changes, these are by no means the only ones. Other stress-based Carite developments mentioned before are Davide's Law and the stress-based raising of Proto-Indo-European _*ē *ō_. Outside of Carite, we find Dybo's Law - the pretonic shortening of vowels in some environments - which most certainly affected Celtic and quite possibly also Latin and Germanic; for more information, please refer to §Matasović5§.
